Business.title: Review launched into how pub and hotel business rates calculated
Business.text:
A review is being launched into the way business rates are calculated for pubs and hotels in England and Wales, and could lead to a reform of the system.

The Treasury says business rates expert Jerry Schurder will lead the review into rate valuations and report back in March 2027, with the government calling for the views of landlords, hoteliers and business owners to feed in to the process.

Last month, Andy Burnham announced a 20% cut in business rates for pubs, social clubs and live music venues in England, to come into effect in April.

Pub groups have argued they face disproportionately higher rates bills, but other businesses have called for a wider reform of the rates system.

According to the British Beer and Pub Association (BBPA), 161 pubs closed in the first three months of this year across England, Scotland and Wales, equating to the loss of around 2,400 jobs.

Rising business rates are cited as one issue facing the sector, although there have also been complaints that increases in National Insurance and the minimum wage have made staff costs more expensive.

James Murray, financial secretary to the Treasury, said the new review would look at "a rethink of valuations - so that we can build a fairer system for the future".

Emma McClarkin, chief executive of the BBPA, said: "For years pubs have paid a disproportionately higher business rates bill which has ground down their ability to keep the doors open, so this review is sorely needed and hugely welcome."

The BBPA says pubs are valued differently for rates than retail venues. Instead of being based just on floor area, they are judged by a measure called Fair Maintainable Trade (FMT) - which means when a pub's turnover increases, so does its rates bill.

Jonathan Lawson, the chief executive of Butcombe Group, which has 120 pubs across the south and south west of England, told the BBC's Today programme that the use of FMT meant pubs were effectively being "punished for success", while large online retailers that operate out of warehouses were not subject to revenue-based rates calculations.

Their rates, he said, "are calculated based on what is deemed to be the market rent for that area, and takes very little on board in terms of revenue driven through that site".

"You can have a very large site paying a relatively low level of business rates versus a relatively small pub... paying a very high level of business rates."

Schurder is a former business rates policy lead at advisory firm Newmark UK, and his review will feed into the next rates revaluation in 2029.

Northern Ireland and Scotland set their own valuations, while Wales presently chooses to align its methodology with England. As the same approach is used across England and Wales, the review will be looking for responses from both nations.

Schurder's appointment was welcomed by Craig Beaumont of the Federation of Small Businesses (FSB) who said he would bring "crucial heavyweight business rates expertise into the Treasury".

However, Beaumont said the government needed to address the wider business rates system and exempt more smaller firms by increasing the rates relief threshold for small businesses.

Jonny Haseldine from the British Chambers of Commerce (BCC) also said the review of valuations should be wider.

"The full reform of business rates, promised by the government at the last election, is urgently needed. This continued piecemeal approach to reform is the wrong approach," he said.

While the BCC said hospitality was the sector most worried about rates, Haseldine warned firms in every sector were struggling with the "complex and outdated" system.

Shadow Chancellor Sir Mel Stride said the review was "far too late for a sector this Labour government has already done its best to kill off".

"Tax hikes on business premises and jobs, alongside job-destroying regulation in the Employment Rights Act, have left many hospitality businesses on the brink," he said.

Liberal Democrat Treasury spokesperson Daisy Cooper said reform of business rates was "long overdue", but also called for an emergency VAT cut and a reverse to jobs tax changes "which have hammered hospitality in particular".

Business.title: 81,000 warning letters sent to crypto holders in HMRC tax crackdown
Business.text:
HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) sent more than 81,000 letters warning cryptocurrency holders they may owe capital gains tax in the past year.

A Freedom of Information (FOI) request seen by the BBC showed the number of letters sent by the tax authority had almost tripled since 2024.

Investors could face fines or prosecution if they fail to declare profits they made from selling, even if they exchange one cryptocurrency for another.

New powers due to be given to HMRC next year will make it easier to target wealthy crypto investors, with one analyst saying investigations will be like "shooting fish in a barrel".

"There is the expectation amongst tax authorities that cryptocurrency investment is rife with tax evasion," says Neela Chauhan, partner at UHY Hacker Young - which carried out the FOI.

"A lot of the traders are young, have had little previous exposure to HMRC and often work under the assumption that HMRC has limited visibility over their activities."

In the 2025-26 financial year, HMRC sent 81,172 warning letters, emails and text messages to crypto investors it suspects may have underpaid tax.

The number in 2023-24 was just 27,714.

An HMRC spokesperson said: "We’re committed to helping people pay the right amount of tax, and the vast majority do.

"We regularly send letters to educate, remind or prompt customers to review their tax affairs, including customers who use crypto assets."

Business.title: US removes Syria from list of state sponsors of terrorism
Business.text:
The US has removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism after 47 years, lifting what it said was the "final major barriers" for private sector investment in the country and its reintegration into the global economy.

US Secretary Of State Marco Rubio said the move was in recognition of the Syrian government's positive actions to fully distance itself from acts of international terrorism.

The Trump administration has embraced Syria's new president, Ahmed al-Sharaa, a former militant who once had an American bounty on his head as the leader of an al-Qaeda off-shoot.

His Islamist group, Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), was also removed from the US list of global terrorist organisations.

HTS, formerly known as al-Nusra Front, was al-Qaeda's affiliate in Syria until Sharaa severed ties with the jihadist network in 2016.

In late 2024, HTS led the rebel offensive that overthrew former president Bashar al-Assad and it dominates Sharaa's transitional administration.

The US hopes to bring Syria into its orbit rather than that of Russia or China. But the risks remain significant, with Syria still far from secure and lacking representative government. It is also at the centre of growing tensions between its neighbours Israel and Turkey.

Rubio said Monday's move, which had been initially flagged in July, would give the Syrian "a path to prosperity".

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said: "Today's action will help foster additional investment in Syria to promote political and economic stability."

Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad Hassan al-Shaibani greeted the news as a "historic step", according to state-run news agency SANA.

"We will continue working to remove the effects of isolation and create an environment based on transparency, mutual interests and respect," he said.

Last year, the US also revoked the designation of HTS as a Foreign Terrorist Organisation and removed Sharaa from its list of Specially Designated Global Terrorists.

Syria's removal from the US list of state sponsors of terrorism - where it had been since 1979 - leaves just three remaining: Cuba, North Korea and Iran.

The listing carries financial sanctions, restrictions on US foreign aid and defence exports and sales and can also penalise people and other countries that trade with the sanctioned state.

Sports.title: Cole Palmer & Morgan Rogers shine in Chelsea win but Robert Sanchez struggles
Sports.text:
If football is won in both boxes, it seems as though Chelsea have one far better covered than the other.

Xabi Alonso began his Stamford Bridge reign with an entertaining 3-2 Premier League win at west London rivals Fulham on Monday - and their new-look front three stole the show.

Morgan Rogers, making his debut after his club record £117m summer move from Aston Villa, combined with Cole Palmer and Joao Pedro to produce a devastating attacking display.

All three scored, with Palmer in particular looking back to his best after a difficult year hampered by injuries, culminating in his omission from England's World Cup squad.

At the other end, though, questions remain over goalkeeper Robert Sanchez after two errors contributed to Fulham's goals from Josh King and Gonzalo Garcia.

Alonso said his front three needed to "lead the rest" so that the "other ones will follow".

But Sanchez has some catching up to do - and when asked about his mistakes, Alonso could only stress the collective responsibility of the team.

"We need to accept and learn from them [the mistakes]," said the Spaniard. "This is going to be a process.

"All the lines, from the strikers, the midfielders, the defence, the goalkeepers, we want to do better in everything."

After the match, ex-Liverpool defender Jamie Carragher - a former team-mate of Alonso - said on Sky Sports that Palmer, Rogers and Joao Pedro are "as good as anything in the Premier League right now".

He also said they would they "will never win the league with Sanchez in goal".

Will that come to pass?

It took Joao Pedro just 31 seconds to open the scoring, latching on to a pass from Palmer and lifting his shot over Fulham goalkeeper Bernd Leno for Chelsea's fastest goal since October 2016.

After King had equalised, Rogers then marked his debut with a goal before half-time by tapping in from close range.

But it was Palmer - scorer of Chelsea's third - who stood out most.

He has endured a frustrating 18 months since a niggling groin problem disrupted his sensational start to life at Stamford Bridge, highlighted by the fact he matched last season's Premier League assist tally by setting up Joao Pedro.

His trickery and creativity was on display throughout against Fulham, along with an impressive work-rate. This was more like the Palmer we saw during his first season at Stamford Bridge - and like the one who tore Paris St-Germain apart during last year's Club World Cup final.

"Over the summer I rested, I recharged and, yeah, I'm ready and I'm hungry," Palmer, who is now just two goals away from 50 in the Premier League, told Sky Sports.

He certainly looks refreshed.

During Chelsea's pre-season tour of Australia, he spoke of having a point to prove and admitted a lengthy summer break felt unusual after featuring in major tournaments in each of the previous three years.

"Cole Palmer was sensational," said former Manchester United defender Gary Neville on Sky Sports. "Him and Morgan Rogers were electric with Joao Pedro - the front three were brilliant.

"That tonight was the old Cole Palmer. It was unbelievable to watch. One of the best things I've seen this weekend."

While Palmer and Joao Pedro have generally carried Chelsea's biggest attacking threat in recent times, they have now been joined by the impressive Rogers too.

His arrival reunites him with Palmer, an ex-Manchester City team-mate and someone he described after the win at Craven Cottage as his "best friend in football".

"He had a difficult season with injuries and stuff last year - and you could see it in his eyes in pre-season and training that he's ready this year and ready to prove people wrong," added Rogers when asked about Palmer's display.

"You saw that with that performance. He was the best player on the pitch by a mile and that's what he does. It's good to have him on our side."

Indeed, it was also encouraging how Rogers, whose pre-season was shortened by his involvement in England's run to third place at the World Cup, looked so fit and powerful.

Rogers is the first Chelsea player to score on his Premier League debut since Christopher Nkunku in 2023 - and the first to create five chances in his first league appearance since records began in 2003-04.

It was also the first time Chelsea supporters sang the new Rogers chant in the away end.

Like Palmer, Joao Pedro missed out on the World Cup - as a high-profile omission from Brazil's squad - but returned in pre-season with eight goals in seven games.

It was no surprise to see him on the scoresheet so early in the Premier League campaign, having inherited the number nine shirt from Liam Delap, who was left out of the squad on Monday, following the contract extension the Brazilian signed this weekend.

"Great combination, great quality," Alonso told BBC Match of the Day when asked about his front three.

"We know if we reach them [Joao Pedro, Morgan Rogers and Cole Palmer] in good positions, they have this talent to create special things and I am very happy the three forwards have scored.

"We need to put them in the best situations. I am happy for the three of them. They played for the team."

Yet questions remain over Sanchez, who allowed King's low strike to go straight through him for Fulham's equaliser and then tamely parried Timothy Castagne's shot into a dangerous area for Garcia to head in from close range to set up a nervy finish.

"They have strengthened in every position of the pitch but you cannot take a chance on goalkeepers," said Neville.

"I've said before it's the most difficult position on the pitch, it's the one that carries the most scrutiny and if you have got a goalkeeper who's making mistakes and is anxious, it will undermine everything you're trying to do.

"It's a problem. You've got to say it's a problem."

There was nowhere to hide for Sanchez.

King's equaliser in the 23rd minute had an expected goals on target (xGoT) value of just 0.05, making it the lowest-rated shot to result in a goal during the opening weekend of the Premier League season.

In other words, Sanchez really should have saved it.

He did make a number of other saves, but he also conceded a corner after failing to clear the ball before it ran out of play and was later unconvincing when coming off his line to deal with a long ball, with Antonee Robinson missing the target to let him off the hook.

While Alonso defended his goalkeeper after the game, in his pre-match news conference on Thursday, he said: "The pitch is the boss of everything. I don't decide. The players need to show me."

That message applied to his goalkeepers - Sanchez and number two Mike Penders, 21, who is waiting to make his debut after returning from a successful loan spell at Strasbourg.

With the transfer window still open, many Chelsea fans will be asking whether the club need a new first-choice goalkeeper.

As Carragher said: "They have to sort the goalkeeping issue out because it's going to come back and haunt them again this season as it did tonight."

Sports.title: Aston Villa: Ollie Watkins transfer saga leaves Villa shellshocked
Sports.text:
Aston Villa have been here before.

Last year, it was Emi Martinez looking to leave for Manchester United. When asked about the Argentina goalkeeper's absence from last season's opening league match against Crystal Palace, head coach Unai Emery just repeated replacement Marco Bizot's name several times.

Twelve months on, for their Premier League opener at Brighton on Sunday, Ollie Watkins was the name to make Emery bristle.

"This question is for him. I can answer only with my silence," he said, when asked why the striker was not included.

That Villa lost 4-0 - conceding all four in a calamitous opening 31 minutes before having debutant Joao Gomes sent off - merely added to the perceived insult.

Saudi Pro League side Al-Hilal have had four offers rejected for Watkins - whose time at Villa now appears to be at a tumultuous end.

Al-Hilal, who have offered close to £40m, are not near to Aston Villa's asking price. As next Tuesday's transfer deadline nears, Villa will play hardball for their all-time record Premier League goalscorer.

A deal is still believed to be some way off, even if Emery revealed last week the striker could leave.

Al-Hilal, who signed Crysensio Summerville from West Ham in July, are likely to need to move one of their overseas players to make room for Watkins, despite loaning Darwin Nunez to Diriyah last week, so there are other moving parts in the deal.

Watkins has been training on his own, having returned from an extended break following the World Cup and is understood to have made his feelings clear to the Villa hierarchy about moving.

There have been no public comments from Watkins or his representatives but he is understood to be open to the move.

They have also kept quiet about Emery's response - particularly his enigmatic "silence" answer to Sky Sports' question on why his striker was not involved at Brighton, which appeared to lay the blame at Watkins' door.

Another unanswered question is whether Villa see the Saudi money for a striker turning 31 in December - and who had been in and out of Emery's team last season - as a good deal.

Perhaps the very real pain at this potential break-up is the reason for the difficulties.

The 30-year-old has 108 goals in 278 games for Villa after joining from Brentford for a then-record £28m and has been synonymous with Villa's rise of the past six years.

The triumphant night in Istanbul, when Watkins helped Villa end their 30-year wait for a trophy as they beat Freiburg to win the Europa League, currently stand as a crowning glory.

His departure would be the most emotional of this summer's big exits - as while Ezri Konsa's influence was crucial, Watkins' goals, work-rate and nature made him one of Villa's poster boys.

He is a grounded and family-orientated individual who enjoys the occasional game of golf but always focuses on his football.

But he has been in this position before, although at a lower level.

Having initially been left out by Paul Tisdale at Exeter amid interest from Derby in 2017, he pleaded with the manager to play and came off the bench to score in a win against Wycombe.

Given he has that attitude and desire, those at Villa are surprised at how the relationship with Watkins is ending. It was not expected to be like this.

Had it been someone different, a player who had previously not been a manager's dream to work with, Emery's response might have been more indifferent.

Sports.title: Brydon Carse: Michael Vaughan says England need punishment to 'send a shiver'
Sports.text:
A punishment to "send a shiver down the whole team" may be needed after Brydon Carse became the latest England cricketer involved in a drinking controversy, according to Michael Vaughan.

Pace bowler Carse was briefly placed under arrest on a night out with his Durham team-mates in Derby at the weekend.

The incident is being investigated by the Cricket Regulator and, as a result, Carse has been removed from the England squad for the second Test against Pakistan at Lord's on Thursday.

"Someone is going to have to get a punishment that sends a shiver down the whole England cricket team and right down through the programme, so that everyone knows that if you misbehave or bring any kind of bad reputation on to this team, you know what's going to come," former England captain Vaughan told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"It's the only punishment that will really hurt players."

In October, England white-ball captain Harry Brook was punched by a bouncer outside a nightclub in Wellington, New Zealand, with team-mates Jacob Bethell and Josh Tongue also present.

During the Ashes tour of Australia, opener Ben Duckett was filmed apparently drunk on England's holiday in Noosa.

And in June, former Test captain Ben Stokes and pace bowler Gus Atkinson broke a team curfew and were present when a member of England's security staff was punched by a Saracens rugby player in a London nightclub.

In this latest incident, Carse was with Durham team-mates Stokes and Matthew Potts, all of whom are under England central contracts. In Stokes' case, the England deal remains in place despite his international retirement in June.

It makes a total of eight contracted players who have been involved in or present for late-night incidents in the past year – more than a quarter of the 30 men on England deals.

In this latest occurrence, footage shared on social media on Sunday showed Carse in handcuffs, surrounded by police officers.

And, although Vaughan said it is an "awful look for the England team once again", he would "feel" for Carse if he is made an example of following the other events of the past year.

"I hope Carse is getting good support around him," said Vaughan. "He is a character who can be a little bit loose and if you give him a bit of rope he'll take a huge amount of it. He needs people around him who are giving him better advice.

"I would feel for Carse if he is the one who takes the rap for what has happened over the past nine months, but somewhere, somehow, something has to be done to set a precedent that they won't stand for that behaviour any more."

On Monday, the England and Wales Cricket Board confirmed that the Regulator was investigating and, as a result, 31-year-old Carse had been removed from the squad for the second Test, with his place going to Sonny Baker.

Soon after that, Derbyshire Police said a man in his 30s was arrested on Saturday night, only to be de-arrested a short time later.

"A man in his 30s was arrested on suspicion of being drunk and disorderly in Derby city centre on Saturday night, 22 August," said a police statement.

"However the man was de-arrested shortly afterwards having agreed to leave the area."

This new controversy comes only one game into Joe Root's second spell as Test captain.

Before his first game back in charge, an innings defeat of Pakistan at Headingley, Root called on his players to be "good role models and good human beings".

Now, Root will speak to the media on Tuesday to address the fallout from the Carse incident.

"Joe Root will be absolutely fuming with this," said Vaughan. "He will have been hoping to arrive at Lord's to talk about cricket and his team.

"Now he will have to answer all these questions about discipline, curfews and drinking culture.

"Everything we thought has been brushed under the carpet and moved to one side, we are pretty much back to square one."

Former England spinner Phil Tufnell agreed with Vaughan that a substantial punishment is the only way to ensure players fall in line.

Tufnell, who had multiple brushes with authority during his international career, said: "If you want to stop this, the only way you stop it is say: 'You're not playing for five games.'

"I was made to stand in the corner during my England career, was told: 'You're not available for selection.' It will soon stop. It would be cleared up in a jiffy."

Carse was in the England squad for the first Test but not selected in the final XI. It is unlikely he would have been in the team for the second Test at Lord's, unless one of England's four frontline seamers from Headingley suffered a fitness issue.

Since Carse made his Test debut in October 2024, no England bowler has more Test wickets than his 58. He was the only member of England's attack to play all five matches in the Ashes series in Australia.

However, he was unavailable at the beginning of the home summer because of an injury, and being removed from the squad for the second Test could push him further down the pecking order.

"Carse is 31 and coming to the autumn of his career," said Tufnell. "You need to keep yourself fit.

"You want to be bowling these long spells for England and making a name for yourself.

"It's probably best not to be doing that [going out so late]. Some of the best in the business have tried and failed at doing that."

Sports.title: US Open 2026 qualifying results: Heather Watson among British winners in New York
Sports.text:
Britain's Heather Watson battled back from a set down against Claire Liu to keep alive her hopes of securing a first US Open main-draw appearance in five years.

The 34-year-old Watson beat sixth seed Liu 4-6 6-2 6-4 in the first round of qualifying in New York.

Watson almost let a double-break lead slip in the final set but held firm to set up a meeting with Spain's Angela Fita Boluda.

Toby Samuel, Jacob Fearnley, Billy Harris and Harry Wendelken all progressed in men's qualifying.

Samuel, seeking to reach the US Open main draw for the first time, fought back against Italy's Francesco Maestrelli to win 6-7 (2-7) 6-3 6-1 and set up a meeting with fellow Briton Harris.

Harris progressed with a 6-1 6-3 win against Peru's Gonzalo Bueno.

Fearnley claimed a 7-6 (7-3) 6-3 victory over Spain's Roberto Carballes Baena to set up a meeting with Frenchman Luka Pavlovic.

Wendelken will meet Swiss player Remy Bertola after overcoming Italy's Stefano Travaglia 6-4 3-6 6-3.

However, Liam Broady lost 7-6 (7-4) 6-3 against Italy's Marco Cecchinato, while Felix Gill was beaten by Italian Francesco Passaro 7-6 (7-3) 6-2.

Players must come through three rounds of qualifying to reach the singles main draw, which gets under way on Sunday.

China's two-time US Open quarter-finalist Zheng Qinwen, contesting a Grand Slam qualifying event for the first time since the 2022 Australian Open, defeated compatriot Xiaodi You 6-3 6-2.

The 23-year-old, who has fallen to 121st in the world since undergoing elbow surgery last year, will meet France's Clara Burel next.

Meanwhile, Brazilian world number 26 Joao Fonseca has announced he will miss the tournament because of an abdominal injury.

The 20-year-old French Open quarter-finalist said he would require "more time to fully recover so I can compete at a high level".

Sports.title: Julian Alvarez transfer news: Arsenal, Barcelona or Atletico Madrid stay for striker?
Sports.text:
Acrimony, anger and animosity: the Julian Alvarez summer transfer saga in a nutshell.

The boos aimed at the Atletico Madrid forward from his own supporters at the Riyadh Air Metropolitano Stadium on Sunday provided the latest twist in what has been one of the most bitter - and certainly public - storylines of the window.

And with deadline day on 1 September, the Argentine World Cup winner's future remains one of the hottest topics.

In simplistic terms the dispute comes down to this: Alvarez wants to join Barcelona - but Atletico won't let him.

The Madrid club's steadfast refusal to sanction the 26-year-old's dream move to the Spotify Camp Nou has led to one of the most rancorous public falling-outs in recent memory.

The feud led to Atleti fans jeering their own player on his return to club action after the summer World Cup in a 2-2 home draw with Villarreal on Sunday.

It had been anticipated.

Atletico Madrid president Enrique Cerezo, speaking last week, said: "I don't know if he will say sorry, but Julian is an excellent person and I am absolutely sure that he will win over the fans in two games.

"I said he wouldn't be sold, he's our player and an important part of our team. We like that he's with us and think he will have a magnificent season."

Nevertheless, the events that unfolded on Sunday certainly haven't gone unnoticed at Arsenal.

BBC Sport has consistently reported over the summer that Alvarez is viewed as the Gunners' dream transfer target.

But for the vast majority of the window, Arsenal's interest has been largely dormant because they were fully aware of his desire to join Barcelona.

They have been waiting for the right moment to strike and those at the Emirates are hopeful that time may be coming.

But is the deal possible?

Arsenal are realistic about their chances of signing Alvarez before next week's transfer deadline.

Do they want him? Yes. Are they trying? Yes. Can they pull it off? The answer to that question is less unequivocal.

Manager Mikel Arteta and sporting director Andrea Berta know it is a long shot, not least because former Manchester City forward Alvarez, at least so far, has shown little indication he would be willing to join the club.

His current reluctance to give the green light on a move to London isn't necessarily linked to any apprehension towards Arsenal - but rather that doing so would see him forgoing his dream of joining Barcelona.

Alvarez has also been made aware of certain visa regulations that would create difficulty for his family visiting him in the UK.

Moving to Catalonia is what he truly wants.

What's more, the Camp Nou club are absolutely willing to make that happen.

But Atleti are absolutely adamant they will not sell Alvarez to Barcelona.

In May, they made a series of social media posts brutally mocking the pursuit by the Spanish champions of their player to millions of followers.

"Don't believe everything you see, especially if it's related to Barca," Atletico posted. "In recent months, we've been suffering a smear campaign against one of our players."

For the Madrid side, the matter is closed and that leaves Alvarez's dream in serious jeopardy.

Therein lies a sliver of hope for Arsenal because, as things stand, the only way out is a move to the Emirates Stadium.

Indeed, according to well-placed sources there has been a slight softening of Alvarez's stance in recent days, although not enough yet to get anyone at Arsenal excited.

But should he change his mind in the final days of the window, then the Gunners are poised.

Since the start of the summer, according to BBC Sport sources, Arsenal have been confident Alvarez's move to Barcelona was a non-starter.

But while he still harboured hope of fulfilling that ambition, Arteta's men focused on the captures of Bruno Guimaraes and Ezri Konsa, while also trying to bring Real Madrid attacker Vinicius Jr to London.

With the Brazilian extending his contract to stay in Spain, Arsenal have now decided to step things up regarding Alvarez.

Atleti director Mateu Alemany was in London last week, where he is understood to have met with Arsenal counterparts - and made clear his side would seek a fee of 150m euros (£128m).

The Gunners are confident they can finance any deal and quickly finalise the transfer - if he said yes.

Arteta is fully aware if Alvarez was to join Arsenal this summer he would only be doing so because his preferred destination was not possible.

It is understood the Spaniard is comfortable with that scenario and believes Alvarez would eventually become fully invested and committed to the Arsenal project.

The ball is now in Alvarez's court. If he wants to leave Atletico, which sources close to the attacker insist that he does, then the Premier League champions appear to be his only option.

Alvarez joined Atletico for £81m from Manchester City in August 2024, having spent just over two years at the Etihad following a £14.1 move from Argentine side River Plate.

He won six major trophies at City - including the Treble of Premier League, FA Cup and Champions League in 2023 - scoring 36 goals in 106 appearances.

At Atletico, he has scored 49 goals in 107 appearances, but has not yet won any silverware.

Could Alvarez also concede defeat in his efforts to leave Atleti this summer and attempt to mend what appears to be a broken relationship with the club and its supporters?

It is possible, although, according to those close to the player, it is his belief that the Madrid club are being unreasonable. Indeed the player's agent Fernando Hidalgo has been open with his disdain towards how his client has been treated this summer.

That said, Alvarez is described as a private individual and said to be deeply uncomfortable about the very public nature of the conflict with his club - although the player himself also outlined his desire to leave publicly during the World Cup.

"A transfer is the best option," he said.

When Real Madrid released a statement on 9 June saying they had an offer of 150m euros (£128m) rejected by their neighbours, there was a sense from the Alvarez camp Atletico had reneged on an agreement to let the striker leave if they received an offer of that amount.

Of course, the prospect of selling Alvarez to their fiercest rivals was viewed as a non-starter by Atletico.

For South Americans - playing for Real or Barca represents the holy grail.

Hansi Flick's side remain interested in Alvarez, but fear Atletico's stance isn't purely posturing and have started to consider alternative options, including Arsenal's Swedish striker Viktor Gyokeres.

If they decide to turn their attention elsewhere, Alvarez will have a decision to make.

Arsenal or nothing? We'll have the answer soon.

Sports.title: Keely Hodgkinson withdraws from Zurich Diamond League as body "not quite ready"
Sports.text:
Keely Hodgkinson has withdrawn from the women's 800 metres at Thursday's Diamond League meeting in Zurich because her "body is not quite ready".

Olympic champion Hodgkinson had been set to go head-to-head with Switzerland's Audrey Werro, who beat the Briton to gold at the European Championships in Birmingham earlier this month.

"Unfortunately the body isn't quite ready to race again after the European Championships," Hodgkinson said in a statement.

"We've made the decision to skip this race and get ready for the next one. Sad to miss it, hopefully see you next year!"

The race will feature world 400m hurdles champion Femke Broeders-Bol, who has stepped up to the 800m this season, and Hodgkinson's training partner Georgia Hunter-Bell, who won 800m gold at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow last month.

World 800m champion Lilian Odira of Kenya, who beat Hodgkinson and Hunter-Bell to gold in Tokyo last year, has pulled out of the race after suffering from illness and weakness since the Commonwealth Games.

While Diamond League organisers said they were looking forward to Hodgkinson's "highly anticipated race against Audrey Werro", they "fully respect" the Briton's decision and "hope to see her back in Zurich in the future".

After suffering hamstring and knee injuries over the past few years, Hodgkinson skipped the Commonwealth Games to prioritise the European Championships amid a busy summer schedule.

"I signed myself up for Zurich because I knew everyone was in it but me. I want to be in with the best and I think that's going to bring out the best in me," Hodgkinson said in Birmingham earlier this month.

Before winning 800m gold at the London Diamond League on 18 July, Hodgkinson said she was feeling "definitely a lot better than I was".

Thursday's meet in Zurich is the penultimate Diamond League event of the season, with the final to take place in Brussels over two days on Friday 4 and Saturday 5 September.

Sports.title: Troy Deeney's Team of the Week: Trafford, Mendy, Guehi, Palmer, Pedro
Sports.text:
After every round of Premier League matches this season, BBC football pundit Troy Deeney will give you his team and manager of the week.

Here are this week's choices.

Do you agree? Give us your thoughts using the comments form at the bottom of this page.

Keane Lewis-Potter (Brentford): He was excellent defensively and attacking wise and got his goal. He is one of Brentford's underrated players and sort of sums up their team. Nobody speaks about him or Brentford but they hammered Tottenham.

Nobel Mendy (Hull City): He was so good and powerful. He offered so much defensively to Hull and scored their second goal. He was a real powerhouse. Hull will definitely need him and he is one of those defenders where you think, 'I don't want to play against him'.

Maxence Lacroix (Chelsea): Lacroix just added a level of experience and calmness to Chelsea and also got an assist. He read the game and understood what was needed and provided the maturity that will add so much to Chelsea going forward. It was a very good debut for the France defender.

Maxim de Cuyper (Brighton): He scored two goals and was excellent for Brighton. Opponents Aston Villa were poor, but if you watched the first 20 minutes you would see he was really aggressive and really set the tone with the pressure.

Marc Guehi (Man City): I'll have Guehi in as my holding midfielder. He should have scored two against Bournemouth because he missed a massive chance before he ended up scoring. But he got the equaliser and offered a lot more of a calming presence than City's £116m record signing Elliot Anderson - Guehi controlled the game a little bit more.

Vitaly Janelt (Brentford): He is one of those big, powerful and dominant players who does the basics really well. He mixed that with a goal against Spurs and you don't really speak about him, but he was always the one breaking up play and doing the horrible things really well.

Christos Tzolis (Arsenal): A lot of people are talking about Arsenal and how they're great. That is absolutely true. And so is the bit of business they did bringing this young man in from Club Brugge. So many goals and assists he brings to the team, but also a calming influence and tenacity as well. Look at Gabriel Martinelli, Leandro Trossard, he feels to me like both of them in one. He has a lot more output than those guys. He's going to be a beast for this year.

Anthony Elanga (Newcastle): Last season I though he was treated poorly by Eddie Howe because he was one that kept being put on the bench, being introduced late or would be the first one to come off. But he showed in a new formation, under a new manager and somebody who believes in him that he can use his pace and power. As a result he looks like a completely different player and he looked happy. He ran past Milos Kerkez like he wasn't there despite the Liverpool left-back having a five-yard start and produced an unbelievable finish for his goal.

Cole Palmer (Chelsea): One we were all talking about, and should've gone to the World Cup with England. Feels like he's got a point to prove, feels like he's been working hard. The injuries from last year skewed everyone's vision. This is going to be a breakout season for him. Everything he did was positive. Ran forward with pace, looked like he could move. He had those issues with the groin but now he's chopping and turning.

Sports.title: Arsenal transfer news: Al-Hilal in advanced talks to sign Gabriel Martinelli
Sports.text:
Arsenal are in advanced talks with Saudi Arabian club Al-Hilal over the sale of Gabriel Martinelli for at least £50m.

The Brazil international, 25, is free to leave the club this summer, with manager Mikel Arteta making it clear the attacker is not in his plans.

Discussions between the clubs have intensified in the last 24 hours, with a deal now close.

If a final agreement is reached, it will be up to Martinelli - who has already turned down a move to Galatasaray - to decide whether he wants to play in the Saudi Pro League.

The wage package Al-Hilal are offering is also understood to be significantly more than his reported £180,000-per-week deal at Arsenal.

Martinelli, who joined Arsenal from Brazilian side Ituano in 2019, has 12 months remaining on his deal at Emirates Stadium.

He made 53 appearances in all competitions last season, scoring 11 goals, as the Gunners won the Premier League title.

But he was left out of the squad for their league opener against Coventry on Friday, which the Gunners won 3-0.

Former Arsenal striker Ian Wright was critical of Arteta's decision to omit Martinelli from the squad, as well as the club's treatment of the forward.

"The way Martinelli is being treated at the moment, it really makes me feel uncomfortable," Wright told Sky Sports.

"I know they might want him out, and a lot of people might say, 'yeah, it's time for him to move him on'. But there's ways of doing that and it should suit him as well, how he wants to leave."

BBC Sport understands Arteta has made his position clear to Martinelli and explained his reasons why he has been left out of the squad.

Al-Hilal's interest in Martinelli runs alongside a move for Aston Villa striker Ollie Watkins.

Sports.title: Liam Delap: Nottingham Forest working on deal for Chelsea striker
Sports.text:
Nottingham Forest are working on a deal to sign Chelsea striker Liam Delap.

The 23-year-old has been made available for sale by Chelsea for £50m and is training separately from the first-team squad.

It remains unclear whether the talks are over a permanent transfer or a loan move, but the two clubs are known to have a positive working relationship.

Delap was left out of Chelsea's squad for Monday's Premier League match against Fulham and lost the number nine shirt to fellow forward Joao Pedro last week.

His potential departure comes just over 12 months after moving to Stamford Bridge for £30m from Ipswich Town, but he ended the season with just one league goal after shoulder and hamstring injuries.

Forest have signed defender Ousmane Diomande from Sporting for £34m, alongside free agents, midfielder Xaver Schlager and keeper Steve Benda, so far this summer.

However, they have sold England midfielder Elliot Anderson to Manchester City for a club-record £116m and striker Taiwo Awoniyi to Coventry City for £9m.

Delap's arrival would provide competition for Chris Wood and Igor Jesus at the City Ground.

Sports.title: Esports World Cup: AG.AL wins tournament in surprise victory
Sports.text:
China-based team AG.AL have been crowned surprise winners of the Esports World Cup (EWC) after seven weeks of competition in Paris.

The team claimed the tournament trophy and $7m (£5.1m) top prize at a ceremony attended by French President Emmanuel Macron, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed Bin Salman and Fifa boss Gianni Infantino.

Bosses moved the contest, which was due to be held in Saudi Arabian capital Riyadh, to France at the last minute due to safety concerns over the conflict between the US and Iran in the Middle East.

The event has attracted criticism from some fans due to Saudi Arabia's ongoing involvement, but organisers the Esports Foundation said it had attracted more viewers this year.

Although it is branded as a World Cup, players in the EWC don't compete for their countries but as individuals or in a team, fighting it out across popular video games such as Call of Duty and League of Legends.

AG.AL clinched victory on the final weekend thanks to French player Gwendal "Gwen" Duparc, whose win on racing game Trackmania put them ahead of reigning champions the Saudi Arabia-based Team Falcons.

Other highlights of the event included 15-year-old Chilean player Jaime "Craime" Bustos winning the Street Fighter 6 tournament to become the youngest-ever EWC champion.

Rocket League pro Samy "dralii" Hajji won a third consecutive EWC victory, while chess grandmaster Magnus Carlsen claimed a second title.

The overall winners' trophy was presented by Macron at the EWC closing ceremony after it was brought on to the stage by footballer Cristiano Ronaldo.

Saudi ruler Bin Salman and Fifa President Infantino watched on as AG.AL's bosses collected the prize.

Though some players, commentators and fans have boycotted the EWC because of Saudi Arabia's involvement, it still proves popular.

Organisers say the event attracts 2,000 players from 100 countries, with some of the world's top esports stars among them.

They claimed this year's EWC reached 850 million viewers across the tournament, with 175,000 tickets sold.

Teams have previously told BBC Newsbeat they "can't afford to ignore" the contest and a potential share of its $75m (£50m) prize pot, as funding for esports is on the decline.

The tournament is run by the Esports Foundation, which describes itself as a non-profit organisation. It was created with the support of the Saudi government, and the EWC launched with an announcement from Bin Salman.

Investing in esports has been a part of the Kingdom's push to become a major player in global gaming - a strategy termed "pixelwashing" by website gamedeveloper.com, external.

The country also recently acquired video game giant Electronic Arts in a record-breaking buyout.

Critics claim it's an attempt to improve the country's international reputation and distract from complaints about its human rights record and anti-LGBT laws.

Saudi Arabia has faced similar accusations of "sportswashing" due to its investments in football, golf and other sports - which it has spent years denying.

Sports.title: Post-Pep Premier League era begins with blast of hyper-managed shock and awe
Sports.text:
There has been something oddly narcotic and moreish about the drip‑drip of fresh Pep Guardiola content either side of the start of the new Premier League season. Eras come and go. Everything dies, baby, that’s a fact. But four‑part Amazon Prime documentaries make angels of us all.

So we have continued to feast on the Pep-at-City visuals: dead jeopardy, reheated beefs, the uplifting team talks of a departed manager to the departed players of a departed team, and moments that often feel far more gripping than the daily churn of what we must, out of habit, call the real world.

The thought occurred watching all this: has the Premier League found its Tupac? Is Pep just going to keep on doing this, dropping new material, fresh hits, posthumous platinum albums? A bald, thin charismatic man who keeps on releasing his lost tapes. We have exactly the thing, sir. Is he even actually dead?

Probably this won’t happen. But a profound absence is still a profound presence at moments like these. The ghosts continue to pull the strings. This weekend was the first of the new Premier League season. More significantly, it was also the first of the post‑Pep era.

And this has been a genuine era, 10 years in the game and an entire tactical culture shift in the making. Unsurprisingly, there was an odd sense of lightness across those nine fixtures on Friday through to Sunday, of old bonds cast aside, even a little giddiness. Suddenly dad isn’t home. The chair by the door is empty. Let’s all just rip it up a bit, shall we?

This relies on a slightly out‑of‑date notion of what Guardiola‑ism became in its later years. But the fact is, something interesting did happen in those Friday‑to‑Sunday games. Think of pure Pep-ball and what are you seeing? Possession. Cold, high‑craft control. This is a coach who famously said: “My desire is to have 100% possession,” after a 5-1 thrashing of Arsenal in Munich during which Thiago Alcântara complete 122 passes.

Admittedly, Guardiola was speaking out of frustration that day, talking more about not losing the ball at key moments, possession as defence. But these ideas did have a profound mimetic effect in England. During Guardiola’s decade at Manchester City the team that had the least possession in the Premier League would win, on average, only 30%-35% of games, a figure that fell as low as 28% in 2021‑22 but which had begun to pick up in the last two seasons as even City’s own version of Pep‑ball became more mixed and next‑gen.

But this weekend the opposite thing happened. In six of nine games played from Friday to Sunday one team took significantly more possession while failing to win. Liverpool had 60% possession plus 27 shots but still just scrambled a draw and looked, frankly, pretty wild. Manchester United had 71% possession and were well beaten by Hull. Tottenham had 60 % possession and lost 3-0. Nottingham Forest had 56% and lost. Sunderland had 62%, Crystal Palace 58%, and both lost.

There were three exceptions to this, all outliers in their own way. Manchester City had 66% possession and won at home against Bournemouth, but spent 84 minutes looking like they were losing. Brighton had 73% possession and beat an Aston Villa team that had made a collective decision to play with their eyes closed and their legs on the wrong way round. Arsenal dominated every metric against a promoted Coventry team that looked, frankly, a little spooked by their first sight of that fresh Everest.

So, a tiny sample size. It may mean absolutely nothing. It could get flipped on its head before we hit September. Also, it is important to note that pure possession stats have rarely dictated with any certainty who will win a game. The top teams always tend to have most of the ball, thus skewing the overall stats.

Otherwise, possession has been a far less reliable guide to victory than, say, expected goals, which speaks clearly to the effectiveness of a system. Whereas simply keeping the ball is often a sign of the opposite of good health, of football as a collective anxiety attack, out there playing with your worry beads, tramping a horseshoe shape into the grass while your opponents mass for the decisive blitzkrieg.

But it wasn’t just the possession numbers that were notable this weekend. The rhythms of the matches were striking. All three Sunday games featured nine or 10 substitutes in the last 40 minutes or so, and a sense of two separate halves, of finishers brought into play, of a broken, episodic tactical to‑and‑fro in response to shifts in the scoreline and the flow. The World Cup also had that pattern. Maybe this is what football is now.

Mainly there was a striking level of targeted physicality, rehearsed blitz-transitions, groups of players running suddenly forward quickly in formation at certain triggering events. Anthony Elanga’s opener for Newcastle captured this best: 12 seconds, two passes, 70 metres covered in a single perfectly straight line, no off‑the‑cuff inventions or what you might call conventional “creativity”, but a perfect moment of planned collective intelligence and breathtaking athleticism.

This was the pattern elsewhere too, games defined by rapid breaks, by powerful players sourced for their ability to win duels and to carry the ball, and a weekend that felt like another ratcheting up in the Premier League’s journey into hyper‑physicality.

Isn’t it a trend? Is this the next stage in the league’s narrow but furiously intense evolution? There are several managers in new jobs who have reputations for the game of sprints, blitz‑ball: most notably Matthias Jaissle at Newcastle and Roberto De Zerbi at what was, on Saturday, the least De Zerbi‑ish of Spurs, a Spurs that seemed to have absorbed only the mouse part – play dead, hide, roll over – of that fast‑breaking cat‑and‑mouse football.

There are two things worth saying about this. This is not a rejection of Guardiolaism and positional play. Keeping the ball was always about preparing for the moments when you don’t have it. Guardiola’s later Manchester City team would often win by direct means.

But pure possession can also be boringly risk-averse, a kind of footballing atrophy where everyone just sits quivering on the touchline like a swarm of beached jellyfish at dusk. The spectacle is more gripping when the emphasis is on those transitions either side of the passing patterns.

More specifically, it is also an interesting development for Pep’s successor at City, Enzo Maresca, Coolio to his Tupac, whose methods are still very much pure Pep origins, based in control of the ball and rigid positionism, like the last soldier still fighting the second world war from inside a bush on Iwo Jima in 1976.

Is Maresca ready for this? Is he even ahead of it? He gave a televised interview at the weekend where he spoke about the tension between control and risk, possession and creativity, and where he defined players being encouraged to run into unexpected positions as “chaos”. On Monday morning there were headlines describing the Premier League weekend in those terms. But this isn’t chaos. We’ve seen chaos. We’ve seen attack ships on fire off the shoulder of Orion, jinking wingers, dogs of war, hitting the space, Lee Chapman, Rod Wallace and Eric Cantona making heavy metal music with two bass guitars and an antique viola. You want chaos. We can give you chaos.

What the Premier League brought at the weekend, the quick breaks, the freedom to attack at selected moments, was more a kind of hyper-managed shock and awe, targeted speed and physicality born out of calculated risk, numbers, data, heavy briefings.

It was also exciting to watch, which is no bad thing in the world’s most tightly contested, space‑averse league. No doubt there will be tightening, a reaction to the reaction, instant counter‑moves and contingency planning. August can also be odd and silly season-ish, the dog days of a World Cup summer. But it did at times feel as if we were in a post‑something moment. If not quite post‑Pep, whose influence will continue to loom, a tactical Machiavelli with plenty of tapes still left in the vault.
Sports.description: There has been something oddly narcotic and moreish about the drip‑drip of fresh Pep Guardiola content either side of the start of the new Premier League season. Eras come and go. Everything dies, baby, that’s a fact. But four‑part Amazon Prime documentaries make angels of us all. So we have continued to feast on...

Sports.title: San Francisco 49ers owner Jed York pleads no contest after arrest at Ohio trailer park
Sports.text:
The San Francisco 49ers owner Jed York has pleaded no contest to two criminal charges after being arrested at an Ohio trailer park over the weekend.

KRON4 News in San Francisco reported that York was initially arrested on suspicion of engaging in prostitution but that count was amended to a charge of disorderly conduct. He was also charged with possessing criminal tools.

A no contest plea is not an admission of guilt but the defendant in question does accept the punishment for the alleged crimes in question. York was sentenced to a day in jail for each count to be served concurrently and was released on Monday morning. He was also fined a total of $1,150 and ordered to complete an online course. The arrest report does not specify what the criminal tools were in York’s case.

According to the New York Post, court documents say York responded to an advert on a website and “arranged to have sexual activity with [a] female in exchange for $140.” York was arrested later arrested at a trailer park in East Palestine, Ohio, on Sunday morning. The East Palestine Police Department and the Mahoning Valley Human Trafficking Task Force were involved in the arrest. York, 46, was born and raised in Youngstown, a 30-minute drive from East Palestine and still has a home in the area.

York is the nephew of former 49ers majority owner Edward J DeBartolo Jr. York took day to day control of the 49ers in 2008 when he became the team’s CEO. After acquiring his mother’s shares, he became the team’s principal owner in 2024.

“As this is a legal matter, which has been resolved, we will not be providing any further comment at this time,” the 49ers said in a statement. The NFL said in a statement that it is “aware of the matter which will be reviewed under the personal conduct policy.”

Since York took over as CEO, the 49ers have reached three Super Bowls but lost each time.

Gaming_Tech.title: China's humanoid robots are stealing the show, but a quieter machine revolution is unfolding
Gaming_Tech.text:
"I take a nap and the world changes," says Chen Tianyu.

His world certainly does. The 28-year-old keeps up with the latest technology by spending his spare time in factories that are switching to automation. That way he knows what to prioritise when teaching his class about artificial intelligence (AI) and robotics.

In front of him, around 30 college students are studying code. One of them is typing furiously as his eyes dart from the screen to the robot: "The idea is it will grab that cylindrical piece and move it over there."

A line of industrial robots are waiting to be programmed, and in another part of the classroom, students are trying to develop robotic medical instruments. As he guides them, Chen declares: "If you are not needed by the world of AI and robotics, then you'll definitely be among those eliminated".

For the people in this room, this is a step - or rather a leap - towards a future that China is meticulously building: Xi Jinping's $20bn (£14.7bn) plan to put his country at the forefront of innovation and in direct competition with the US.

The evidence is all around them. They are in the Hangzhou Technician Institute, one of several huge, purpose-built vocational schools that want to churn out the next generation of tech-savvy engineers. The campus sits on the outskirts of Hangzhou, a former imperial capital whose futuristic skyline is just the first hint of its role as a global tech hub.

Across the country, there are more than two million robots working in China's factories - which is more than anywhere else - and they are continuing to scale up at extraordinary speed.

It is a commitment that will surely change the world, much like the last time the Chinese economy underwent a massive transformation. It is already shipping its robots across the globe: more than half of the world's industrial robots are now made in China.

What is less clear is the impact of such sweeping automation in a country that sits at the heart of global manufacturing, trade and innovation. What does this mean for China's human workforce, for instance? And how would we be able to truly measure the cost of this transformation in a regime that controls information so tightly?

The future of China's workers is uncertain in the industrial revolution the world has been watching: gleaming solar grids, peak hours made noiseless by electric vehicles, machines that run faster than Usain Bolt. Over the weekend, China hosted the second edition of the World Humanoid Games where robots boxed, sprinted and marched.

What is fuelling this spectacle is another, less visible revolution happening inside factories and classrooms.

The BBC has visited industrial sites where we have been shown robots that do not look human, or dance or leap on stage but weld, paint, lift, assemble and work around the clock without a break or benefits. Some are designed to build more robots. We have also been inside academies where China is training the people who will work alongside its robotic workforce.

This is a front-row seat to what Xi calls China's "new productive forces" - and how they could reshape the country.

On a factory floor in the southern city of Chengdu, the old and and the new are working side by side.

An assembly line of around 30 middle-aged men and women is screwing, drilling and polishing CRP Technology's signature product: a robotic arm which performs various industrial tasks. Also in the room are four young engineers crowded around a console, trying to crack the code for a prototype, a new robot that they hope will help build other robots.

One of them, 31-year-old Pang Kai, who is part of the research and development team, pushes the sleek skeleton across the room. Because China's future workforce is not quite ready to strut out. For now, it can only do simple repetitive movements, such as scan a QR code.

"Maybe in another half year, it can do another task," Pang says, smiling wistfully. It's a long road and the team are celebrating every small win.

CRP Technology, which employs around 300 people, has been building robot arms for nine years. Each arm can be tailored to a factory's needs to help build cars, electronics or wind turbines. The firm says a single arm can be programmed to perform more than 90% of repetitive tasks.

The engineers also wonder if, one day, they can replace the company's workforce. "We want our new robot to be like human beings. We hope it can think by itself," says Pang. "We need these kinds of robots because maybe in 10 years, we won't have enough workers in China."

A shrinking population and an ageing workforce is another reason Beijing is in a hurry to revolutionise its factories. By 2035, more than a third of China's population will be over 60, according to official estimates. The country will also lose nearly 60 million people in the next decade - almost equivalent to the population of France - according to some estimates.

The hope is that increased automation will fill this looming gap in the workforce before it starts to affect an already sluggish economy. But the speed of the transition is key. Around 120 million people still work in the manufacturing sector. If China moves too quickly, job losses could follow dealing a catastrophic blow to millions who depend on factory wages.

"In theory, machines can work 24 hours a day, which is certainly an advantage compared with human workers. But machines also require maintenance. Every day we need time for that, and each month the production line also requires inspection and repair," says Cao Li, vice-president of EV maker Leapmotor.

Increasingly popular in Europe and the UK, the company's budget-friendly, tech-focused cars come together at the Hangzhou factory with robots aiding the process at every step. At the end of the assembly line, more humans emerge.

The company has more than 25,000 workers and hundreds of them make the final checks as the sparkling new vehicles roll past. Will there be a day when they are no longer needed?

"It's entirely possible," Cao says. "And it may come relatively quickly. In workshops, including stamping, welding, and painting, we've basically achieved 100% automation."

China has the edge over the US due to its enormous manufacturing base. Motors, batteries, electronics, gears, sensors - everything needed to build the body of a robot is all at hand.

"China also has an idea. It has a plan. They know where they want to be in five years. They plan at a top level, but they break it down to the regions, to the municipalities," says Dr Susanne Bieller, General Secretary of the International Federation of Robotics.

"If you want to build a robot in Shenzhen - there's an entire ecosystem. It takes you less than one hour to source the components you need to make a robot. In Europe it can take you up to a week."

However, she acknowledges that while China is good at building the body, the US is still leading at building the "brain", which includes developing the AI to programme robots. And yet Chinese firms, from DeepSeek to Moonshot, have been unveiling new AI models that they say can compete with top US firms.

Driven by an "open-source" approach, where AI start-ups share their code, Chinese innovation has been able to catch up faster than expected, despite US export controls over critical advanced chips. Analysts now believe that the next leg of this race will be determined not by who has the best language model, but who can put this intelligence into millions of machines.

And that is why China is also investing in producing a generation of students learning to imagine what could come next.

At the Hangzhou Technician Institute, for example, children can start from the age of 15. And the scale of what is being taught can feel staggering. There is an entire building dedicated to engines and aeronautics, and a restricted floor for students who will work to keep China at the forefront of processing rare earths - another crucial commodity in the battle with Washington.

Some see this as a solution to China's stubbornly high youth unemployment rate, with one in five struggling to find a job. "Our students are in demand and can even be pre-booked by companies. They don't need to worry about employment at all, and we hold competitions as part of their training," Chen, the young teacher, says.

"It's better to find your position within the technological wave. In the process of progress, structural changes are bound to occur, and these structural changes are exactly where students' future employment opportunities lie."

But China still faces serious economic challenges, from a property crisis that continues to drag on to huge local government debt and persistently low consumption.

It is unclear if and how the revolution Beijing is touting will fix these, and it is hard to gauge how those whose jobs are threatened feel about the change that is coming. Will robots create prosperity for them, or simply take many of their jobs?

"My students ask me what will happen in the future," Chen says. "I say I don't know. Technology is changing so fast. But we can't just stand still and sleep here. We have to move forward to see what we are capable of doing."

Gaming_Tech.title: Esports: How to get £2,000 to play computer games at university
Gaming_Tech.text:
As parents across the country prepare to wave their children off to university, conversations about family finances and the cost of living are growing ever more frequent - and fervent.

Yet every year, millions of pounds worth of scholarships and bursary funding goes unclaimed by students - with many unaware the extra help exists.

So roll up the next generation of gamers, who this year can apply for as esports scholarship from the University of Roehampton - with more than 100 handed out so far.

But can the students balance their studies and their esports? And is the scholarship set to catch on?

Esports, meaning electronic sports, is the name for competitive video gaming.

It is different from standard video gaming as esports includes spectators, much like traditional sports.

Gamers compete against one another in high-stakes tournaments for cash prizes and trophies.

Roehampton is offering esports scholarships to undergraduate and postgraduate students who show that they can balance academic progress and video-gaming excellence.

"This scholarship is about recognising talent in a field that has a growing popularity both around the world and among our students," former University of Roehampton registrar Mark Ellul said.

Scholars are expected to compete in weekly university tournaments as well as representing the university at in-person events.

Roehampton requires minimum rankings in major games for the scholarship, but will consider applications from those close to the threshold who meet other criteria, such as having large followings on streaming platforms like Twitch.

Former esports scholar Cameron Dray found out about Roehampton through the esports scholarship. Inspired by similar initiatives at American universities, he looked into whether anything similar was on offer in the UK.

Initially, the university was offering just £1,500, but due to the team's performance and rise in popularity, the amount was raised to £2,000.

"This money was crucial to me as it gave me the opportunity to study in a very expensive city without the need for part-time work," Dray said.

"There were requirements that came alongside the scholarship, but none that were unexpected or not transparent when applying," he added.

Dray encouraged students to make use of every scholarship, bursary and opportunity available to them.

He said: "Many of these funds are available to more students than they realise, and everyone should be taking full advantage."

The average graduate in England leaves university with debts of more than £47,500. Scholarships such as Roehampton's can reduce student debt and provide additional financial support.

Thomas Cole, an esports player nicknamed Pac who specialises in the racing game Trackmania, said universities offering unique scholarships, including esports, encourages students academically by reducing the level of financial stress they might face.

"Uni students being paid to play a game alongside doing their studies, it's definitely cracking. If I had gone to uni, I would have loved that," he says.

"If it doesn't let the academic side suffer, then I think being offered something like that really spurs on people to be better in gaming," he says.

Tom Allingham, student money expert from the Save the Student personal finance site, regularly advises incoming first years to seek out scholarships and learn more about what their university offers.

"Unfortunately, I don't think there is enough awareness on scholarships," he said.

"There is a lot of funding that goes unclaimed because students don't know that they're eligible for it," he added.

Save the Student helps share various scholarships and bursaries on their website.

"What we try to get across is you can get extra funding for so many different reasons."

Gaming_Tech.title: Sharing dangerous driving videos is 'truly reprehensible', PM says
Gaming_Tech.text:
The government has urged social media companies to remove posts celebrating dangerous driving, as Prime Minister Andy Burnham branded sharing them "truly reprehensible".

Earlier Defence Minister Luke Pollard told BBC Breakfast that "social media companies could take the content down easily and adjust their algorithms to stop it being distributed".

Two police officers died when a car going the wrong way down a dual carriageway crashed into their vehicle near Middlesbrough on Saturday. Five passengers in the other car were also killed.

A TikTok account believed to belong to one of the five passengers, 18-year-old Makai Saddington, previously shared videos appearing to show dangerous driving, which have since been removed.

But Cleveland Police said "there is no evidence to indicate that filming of the activities that took place on Friday night and Saturday morning has taken place for the purposes of TikTok".

Pollard said the government had "already taken steps" to tell social media companies to take down such content.

He added: "They know exactly what content is on their site, they know how their algorithm works.

"They also know that people post content to get views and the more views you get, sometimes you get money for it, so it's a financial incentive to post outrageous content that gets more people watching it."

Speaking to reporters in Kyiv, Burnham said the people who share footage glorifying dangerous driving are "doing something that's truly reprehensible".

A Downing Street spokeswoman said "the glorification of dangerous driving for clips and entertainment is utterly disgraceful".

She added that the culture secretary has been clear that footage should be removed by social media platforms "in line with their legal obligations", and that Ofcom has the government's "full backing to take action" against those that fail in their duties.

Video content featuring illegal activity is not necessarily illegal itself - according to the Online Safety Act - it is up to the social network to decide whether flagged content is illegal and act accordingly.

TikTok said its policies prohibit content that could cause significant physical harm, including dangerous driving.

It added that it is actively removing videos and accounts that break its rules, including the account believed to belong to Saddington.

The company said between January and March 2026, 99.8% of the content removed for violating those policies it took down proactively.

While TikTok is taking some videos down, it is not necessarily because it has deemed them to be illegal - it may only be because they breach the firm's own terms and conditions.

There are specific exceptions which are set out in the Online Safety Act, but they can be difficult to interpret.

For example, content showing someone being killed is not necessarily illegal unless it is being shared by a terrorist group, and/or accessible to children.

Facebook and Instagram owner Meta said it prohibits posts encouraging participation in high-risk challenges, including driving against traffic, and takes down such content once made aware.

It said it also restrict users under 18 from seeing content not suitable to them, such as posts depicting any sort of reckless driving.

The BBC has also contacted X for comment.

On Saturday, PC Tom Clough, 38, and PC Matthew Blades, 37, died when a Volkswagen Passat, which officers had been pursuing until seconds before, collided with their marked armed response car on the A66 near Middlesbrough.

All five of the Passat's occupants - Saddington, Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jacob Matusiak, 23, Theo Rae, 17, and Cole Robert Worthy, 17 - also died.

A video posted on the TikTok account believed to belong to Saddington in March 2025 showed him and four other young people involved in what appears to be a police pursuit. The video has since been deleted.

BBC Verify analysed the 94 second-long clip, which showed the car driving on footpaths and parkland in Ormesby, Middlesbrough, with Saddington a rear-seat passenger.

Another video posted by the same account, also since deleted, appears to show a joyride where a passenger is smoking, with the speedometer showing 100mph.

Then, later in the video, a different car is set on fire. The passengers in this video are not identifiable.

Cleveland Police and Crime Commissioner Matt Storey said: "Without being able to say whether that was anything like involved in this case, it's absolutely idiotic for anybody to be doing anything other than being completely 100% focused on the road when they're behind the wheel of a vehicle."

He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that someone filming themselves or others driving dangerously is "absolutely ridiculous, and of course nobody should be doing that".

"It is a worrying situation if that's becoming more prevalent because it is incredibly dangerous", he added.

Earlier this month, five teenagers were killed in a head-on collision in County Kildare, Ireland, after driving the wrong way down a motorway.

They hit a car which was believed to be carrying a family heading to the airport for a holiday. As of Friday, three women and a seven-year-old boy were still in hospital where they were being treated for serious injuries.

At the time, Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly called it "irresponsible and dangerous driving".

He said: "What makes this reckless behaviour even more appalling is that in some cases it is being done for social media likes regardless of the potentially devastating impact it might have on innocent people and themselves."

Speaking to BBC Radio 5Live, Pollard said he wanted to see social media companies "step up".

He added: "It's one of the reasons they've argued against some of the regulations, saying they can police themselves.

"Well this is the perfect opportunity to demonstrate it. Remove the content that celebrates dangerous behaviour on our roads."

The minister said the government will use powers in the Online Safety Act to compel platforms to take down any content that remains online.

A spokesperson for regulator Ofcom said under the act platforms "must minimise children's exposure to violent material and content promoting dangerous challenges".

They added that in July, it launched an investigation "into TikTok's compliance with its child safety duties, and we've shown we'll take action if evidence suggests companies are falling short."

Gaming_Tech.title: Twitch and Amazon face lawsuit over use of streamers' content to train AI
Gaming_Tech.text:
Amazon is facing a lawsuit, external over its move to train its AI models on videos people broadcast on the popular streaming platform Twitch.

The move faced backlash from users when it was announced in August - with people having the option to opt-out if they do not want their data used this way.

The class action lawsuit has been brought on behalf of millions of streamers who use Twitch, alleging its parent company Amazon used their videos to train AI without their permission or proper compensation.

Twitch and Amazon have not commented on the lawsuit.

Streamers on the platform reportedly produced, external more than 215 million hours of content in the first few months of 2026 alone.

The lawsuit was brought by Connecticut-based streamer Warren Pandiscia.

It claims Twitch breached its contract with users by using that content as AI training data for Amazon's models without obtaining their permission.

It adds streamers should not have their work commercially exploited to develop AI without consent or compensation.

The lawsuit seeks damages for streamers whose content was allegedly used to train AI, as well as an order preventing Amazon from continuing the alleged practice.

It is not clear when Amazon began collecting Twitch users' data to train its AI models.

Twitch's chief product officer Mike Minton previously said he did not know if users' data had been scraped for training before it gave people the opportunity to opt-out.

He said he was unsure what Amazon "has done in terms of model training and what they've used and not used".

In Twitch's own FAQs about AI training, it said a person's audio might be used to "refine models that create speech to text".

It said this would help improve automatic subtitles on Twitch streams as well as Amazon videos.

Those that want to disable the feature would need to navigate to the Settings tab in their Streamer Dashboard, click the Security and Privacy tab, then scroll down to near the bottom of the options and toggle off "training for Generative AI".

However, the opt-out only applies to individual streams, meaning creators' content could still be used for AI training when they appear in a stream where the feature remains enabled.

Amazon, which bought Twitch for nearly $1bn (£740m) in 2014, has made AI a major focus as it competes with Google, Meta and other tech giants.
